A microscopy staining method that utilizes toluidine blue, a solution composed of tolonium chloride, to determine the presence of mast cells, lignin, proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans.
A method in which pressure is applied to the surface of the cornea in order to flatten a prespecified area of the membrane.
A procedure involving irradiation of the whole body.
A diagnostic radiologic test that involves the examination of the entire body in a single procedure.

A method of assessing capillary fragility that is used in the diagnosis of hemorrhagic fevers. After taking a blood pressure measurement, the cuff is inflated to a point midway between the assessed systolic and diastolic pressures and maintained for five minutes; the cuff is then released and, after two minutes, the number of petechiae below the antecubital fossa are counted.
An in vitro assay to measure antibody in a biological specimen capable of protecting cells against the effect of a specific toxin.
An ultrasound imaging technique in which the ultrasound probe is pressed against the skin of the abdomen in order to create an image of the abdominal organs.
A technique used to selectively replicate nucleic acid sequences from RNA templates using reverse transcriptase and RNA polymerase.
A cardiac ultrasound performed by passing a specialized probe containing a transducer into the patient's esophagus.
An electron microscopy imaging technique that is utilized to examine structural components of a sample by passing electrons through the specimen.
A non-invasive cardiac ultrasound performed by placing the transducer on the chest.

A technique in which sound waves are sent out by an ultrasound probe that has been inserted in the vagina and a computer uses the ultrasound echoes to create an image of the female reproductive organs.

A microscopy staining method that utilizes two or more colored, acidic dyes of contrasting colors. Masson trichrome is a mixture of three dyes including aniline blue, Beibrich scarlet and Weigert's iron hematoxylin. Other related, modified trichrome staining methods include Lillie's trichrome, Gomori's trichrome and Mallory's trichrome.
A type of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in which images are taken during three distinct timing points (phases) following the injection of contrast material: arterial, venous, and delayed.
A type of computed tomography (CT) in which images are taken during three distinct timing points (phases) following the injection of contrast material: arterial, venous, and delayed.
A microscopy staining method that utilizes trypan blue, an acid azo dye that can traverse the cell membrane of dead cells and is used to differentiate between living and dead cells. (NCI)
A method to quantify the opaqueness of a liquid using a turbidimeter, by measuring the decrease in light intensity due to the scattering effect of suspended particles in the liquid sample.

CDISC Synonym(s): Dual-channel Microarray; Two-channel Expression Array; Two-channel Microarray; Two-color Microarray-based Gene Expression
CDISC Definition: A genomic microarray-based method using cDNA from two samples, labeled with two separate fluorophores/dyes at different emission wavelengths, and hybridized to a single microarray. The relative fluorescence intensity of each dye is being measured.
A technique that measures energy transmission through the middle ear using a tympanometer.
An analytical technique where ultra-high performance liquid chromatography is coupled to accelerated mass spectrometry in order to separate, identify, and quantify substances in a sample.
NCI Preferred Term: Ultra High Performance Liquid Chromatography/Accelerator Mass Spectrometry

CDISC Definition: An analytical technique where ultra-high performance liquid chromatography is coupled to tandem mass spectrometry in order to separate, identify, and quantify substances in a sample.
NCI Preferred Term: Ultra High-performance Liquid Chromatography/Tandem Mass Spectrometry

CDISC Definition: A noninvasive technique that is used to measure organ or tissue stiffness. An ultrasound wave is passed into the organ or tissue from a small transducer on the end of an ultrasound probe which measures the velocity of the shear wave (in meters per second) as this wave passes through the organ or tissue. The shear wave velocity can then be converted into organ or tissue stiffness. This technique may be used as an alternative to organ or tissue biopsy.
A technique in which high-frequency sound waves are bounced off internal organs and the echo pattern is converted into a 2 dimensional picture of the structures beneath the transducer.
A microscopy staining method that utilizes uranyl acetate, a water insoluble yellow crystalline solid, which is used as a negative stain in electron microscopy.

A chemical titration method described by van de Kamer, et al. in 1949 in which fecal fat is quantitatively measured by conversion of fecal lipids into fatty acids through saponification with ethanolic potassium hydroxide, release of the free fatty acids by the addition of hydrochloric acid and extraction into ether, and titration of the fatty acids against sodium hydroxide. (NCI)
A nuclear imaging test that uses radiopharmaceuticals to produce an image of the blood flow to the lungs.

An assay that is used to determine viral quantity by infecting monolayers of host cells with serially diluted virus, covering the monolayers with an immobilizing overlay after a period of incubation to restrict the spread of the virus to neighboring cells, and counting the resulting visible plaques of infected cells.
A psychometric response scale to assess subjective characteristics or symptoms, which relies upon a continuum of possible result values in between two fixed end-points.
Human evaluation of an attribute of a subject or material using visual discernment.
A type of conditioned audiometry to detect sound, where a delayed visual presentation is used to support a child's reflexive orientation response to a audio signal from a single source.

A type of blood cell analysis that uses impedance, conductivity, and laser scatter to measure cell volume, cell size, chemical composition, nuclear volume, cellular granularity, nuclear structure, and cell surface characteristics.
A method for estimating body surface area of second and third degree burns, based on assigned percentages for different regions of the body.

A microscopy staining method that utilizes a modified trichrome stain to determine the presence of microspordial, sporulating species. The staining method utilizes chromotrope 2R, a red acidic dye, the counterstain fast green, and phosphotungstic acid.

A technique that assesses auditory function and/or type of hearing loss, in which a vibrating tuning fork (typically at 256Hz or 512Hz) is placed on top of the head or over the upper lip and the subject reporting whether sound is heard equally in both ears or whether the sound is louder in one ear.
A method that measures the sedimentation rate of an entity in an aqueous solution using a Westergren tube.

A method for the detection or identification of proteins or peptides that have been separated by gel electrophoresis and transferred onto nitrocellulose or other type of paper or nylon membrane. The proteins are then detected by reaction with enzymatically labeled or radiolabeled antibody probes.
A DNA sequencing technique in which all of the exons of an individual's genome are sequenced.
A DNA sequencing technique in which the entirety of the individual's genome is sequenced.

CDISC Synonym(s): RNA-Seq; Whole Transcriptome Shotgun Sequencing; WTSS
CDISC Definition: An RNA sequencing technique in which all of the RNA transcripts of an individual's genome are sequenced.

A microscopy staining method that utilizes the Romanowsky stains, eosin and methylene blue, solubilized in methanol. In this staining protocol, methanol is also utilized as a fixative agent prior to staining.

A microscopy staining method that is a combination of the Wright and Giemsa staining protocols and utilizes the Romanowsky stains, which are mixtures of eosin and thiazine dyes such as methylene blue. It produces darker blue and magenta shades than the giemsa stain alone, which may provide better contrast in microscopy.

A spectrometric method that determines the type and concentration of elements or chemicals in a sample, based upon the principle that each element emits fluorescent light of a particular wavelength when exposed to an X-ray.
A type of X-ray in which the images are not enhanced by the addition of contrast agents into the body.
A radiographic procedure using the emission of x-rays, a type of penetrating energy wave.

A microscopy acid fast staining method that utilizes Ziehl-Neelsen carbol fuchsin, acid alcohol and methylene blue, to determine the presence of acid fast microorganisms. This acid fast staining technique requires heating during the primary staining step involving the carbol fuchsin.
NCI Preferred Term: Ziehl Neelsen Acid Fast Staining Method

CDISC Definition: Terminology relevant to the additional descriptions of the test being performed to produce the microbiology finding.
NCI Preferred Term: CDISC SDTM Microbiology Findings Test Details Terminology

CDISC Definition: A measurement of the total cells of a pre-specified type in a specimen.
A measurement of the total number of microbial colonies of a pre-specified microorganism in a specimen.
The determination of presence or absence of an entity in a specimen.

The further determination and/or classification of the identity of a pre-specified entity or group of entities in a specimen. In the context of microbiology, this is likely the identification of (but is not limited to) genus, species, strains, variants, serotypes, serogroups, genotypes, etc., of a known microorganism(s).

An act or process of elucidation; explication, or explanation of the meaning of the event or thing via the assignment of objects from the domain to the constants of a formal language, truth-values to the proposition symbols, truth-functions to the connectives, other functions to the function symbols, and extensions to the predicates, if any. The assignments are result of human logic application and are not native to the symbols of the formal language.

CDISC Synonym(s): Cp Number; Crossing point Number; Ct; Ct Number; Cycle Threshold; Cycle Threshold #; Cycle Threshold Number; Elbow Value; Take-off Point Number; Threshold Cycle; Threshold Cycle Number; TOP Number
CDISC Definition: The cycle number where the fluorescence of the target is detected above the background signal or a pre-set threshold. This value may be used for the computation of the concentration of a target in a polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
The determination of the quantity of a pre-specified analyte in a specimen.
A measurement of the total number of viral particles of a pre-specified virus in a specimen.
Terminology relevant to the test codes that define microorganism responses to antimicrobial agents.
NCI Preferred Term: CDISC SDTM Microbiology Susceptibility Test Code Terminology

CDISC Synonym(s): Diameter of the Kill Zone; Diameter of the Zone of Inhibition
CDISC Definition: A measurement of the diameter of the circular region of bacteria growth inhibition that surrounds an antibiotic source on the surface of a cultured plate.
An indication as to whether the pre-specified mutations of interest are present in the subject.

An indication of reduced or increased susceptibility of a microbial organism, or activity of a biological/biochemical reaction in response to the inhibitory concentration (IC50 and/or IC95) of a specific drug.

CDISC Synonym(s): Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Baseline
CDISC Definition: A fold change based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition of population growth or replication of a microbial organism. (NCI)
NCI Preferred Term: Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Baseline

CDISC Synonym(s): Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Ref; Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Reference
CDISC Definition: A fold change based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition of the population growth or replication of a microbial organism. It is a ratio calculated by the EC50 Subject Result divided by the EC50 Reference Control Result. (NCI)
NCI Preferred Term: Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Reference

CDISC Definition: A reference control sample response based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition of the population growth or replication of a microbial organism. (NCI)

A measurement of titer of a microbial organism that has been exposed to the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition of the population growth or replication of a microbial organism. (NCI)
A measurement that specifies the minimum concentration of the agent at which organism growth was inhibited.

CDISC Synonym(s): Microbial IC50 Fold Change from Baseline
CDISC Definition: A fold change based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism. It is a ratio calculated by the current IC50 Subject Result divided by the IC50 Subject Result from the baseline visit.
NCI Preferred Term: Microbial IC50 Fold Change from Baseline

CDISC Synonym(s): Microbial IC50 Fold Change from Ref; Microbial IC50 Fold Change from Reference
CDISC Definition: A fold change based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism. It is a ratio calculated by the IC50 Subject Result divided by the IC50 Reference Control Result.
NCI Preferred Term: Microbial IC50 Fold Change from Reference

CDISC Definition: A reference control sample response based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism.

A measurement of biological/biochemical reaction of a microbial organism that has been exposed to the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism.

CDISC Synonym(s): IC95 Fold Change from Baseline; Microbial IC95 Fold Change from Baseline
CDISC Definition: A fold change based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 95 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism. It is a ratio calculated by the current IC95 Subject Result divided by the IC95 Subject Result from the baseline visit.
NCI Preferred Term: Microbial IC95 Fold Change from Baseline

CDISC Synonym(s): IC95 Fold Change from Reference; Microbial IC95 Fold Change from Ref
CDISC Definition: A fold change based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 95 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism. It is a ratio calculated by the IC95 Subject Result divided by the IC95 Reference Control Result.
NCI Preferred Term: Microbial IC95 Fold Change from Ref

CDISC Synonym(s): IC95 Reference Control Result; Microbial IC95 Reference Control Result
CDISC Definition: A reference control sample response based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 95 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism.

CDISC Synonym(s): IC95 Subject Result; Microbial IC95 Subject Result
CDISC Definition: A measurement of biological/biochemical reaction of a microbial organism that has been exposed to the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 95 percent inhibition on the enzymatic activity of a microbial organism.
A phenotypic or genotypic assessment of the response of the microbial organism to an antimicrobial agent.
An indication as to whether one or more scored mutations of interest that may confer susceptibility in the microorganism is present.
Terminology relevant to the test names that define microorganism responses to antimicrobial agents.
NCI Preferred Term: CDISC SDTM Microbiology Susceptibility Test Name Terminology

CDISC Submission Value: Diameter of the Zone of Inhibition
CDISC Synonym(s): Diameter of the Kill Zone; Diameter of the Zone of Inhibition
CDISC Definition: A measurement of the diameter of the circular region of bacteria growth inhibition that surrounds an antibiotic source on the surface of a cultured plate.
An indication as to whether the pre-specified mutations of interest are present in the subject.

An indication of reduced or increased susceptibility of a microbial organism, or activity of a biological/biochemical reaction in response to the inhibitory concentration (IC50 and/or IC95) of a specific drug.

CDISC Submission Value: Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Baseline
CDISC Synonym(s): Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Baseline
CDISC Definition: A fold change based on the concentration of a specific drug expected to produce 50 percent inhibition of population growth or replication of a microbial organism. (NCI)
NCI Preferred Term: Microbial EC50 Fold Change from Baseline

The therapeutic use of cold or refrigeration.

The removal of tissue with a curette (a spoon-shaped instrument with a sharp edge).
A type of digital fundus photography that makes use of a significantly wider viewing angle than traditional fundus photography.
A type of ECG gated MRI in which the images are not enhanced by the addition of contrast agents into the body.
A type of magnetic resonance imaging in which data is acquired during a specified portion of the cardiac cycle, allowing for the collection of stop motion imaging of the heart.
A procedure for destroying tissue using an electrical current.
Excision of an atheromatous plaque. (NCI)
An endoscopic procedure that visualizes the upper part of the gastrointestinal tract up to and including the duodenum.
The act of cutting out; the surgical removal of part or all of a structure or organ. (NCI)
Creation of a surgical opening into the abdominal cavity for examination of the contents of the abdominal cavity as a means of diagnosis.
A type of radiation therapy in which high-energy beams are delivered to the tumor from outside of the body.
The use of an adsorbing hemofilter in an external blood purification device to reduce cytokine levels in the blood.
A technique that utilizes a device to pump a patient's blood outside of the body, oxygenate it, and return it to the body.
Any surgical procedure performed for the purpose of repairing or replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, or dysfunctional heart valve.
A therapeutic procedure that involves the transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells, either with the patient as their own donor or from a donor to a patient.
A therapeutic procedure involving the extracorporeal removal of harmful waste and fluids from the blood using a dialysis machine. Following dialysis, the blood is returned to the body.

A mechanical fluid removal technique that involves the pressure-driven movement of plasma water and solutes from whole blood through a system of extracorporeal filters, with simultaneous reinfusion of replacement fluid into the body to keep volume homeostasis.
A type of brachytherapy that targets a cancerous tissue with high doses of radiation through the use of inserted temporary implants.
The delivery of heated, humidified, oxygen-enriched gas via nasal cannula at flow rates greater than those typically delivered by standard-flow oxygen devices.

An electrocardiographic method for collecting continuous ECG waveforms with a variable number of discrete leads with duration longer than the standard 10 second ECG. Holter recording may be performed in patients who are ambulatory, and may collect data for 24 hours or longer.
A therapy designed to induce changes in a patient's immune status.
A procedure involving an electronic device implanted in the body that delivers electrical stimulation to the heart to treat tachycardia. It may also have the capability to treat bradycardia.
The use of an intense beam of light, such as a laser, to seal off blood vessels or destroy tissue. (NCI)

An advanced form of 3-Dimensional Conformal Radiation Therapy (3D CRT) that involves the use of varying intensities of small radiation beams to produce dosage distributions that are more precise than those possible with 3D CRT. (NCI)

A type of mechanical circulatory support procedure in which a balloon catheter inserted into the proximal descending aorta is inflated immediately after aortic valve closure in diastole and deflated just before aortic valve opening in systole, with the augmentation of coronary blood flow during diastole increasing coronary blood flow and systemic perfusion.
A type of mechanical ventilation procedure that uses an invasive means, such as an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy tube, to deliver oxygenated air into the lungs.
A procedure involving one or more wires used for pacemaker or implantable defibrillator devices.
The therapeutic blockage of the muscular pouch in the left atrium.

CDISC Definition: Surgical removal of the left portion of the colon.

An examination and assessment of the inability of the left ventricle to effectively pump blood to the body.
NCI Preferred Term: Left Cardiac Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction Evaluation

CDISC Definition: Surgical removal of a lobe of an organ.
Any immunotherapy that targets, or is restricted to, a specific anatomical location.
Resection of the rectum through an incision in the lower abdomen.
A type of brachytherapy that targets a cancerous tissue with low doses of radiation through the use of inserted temporary or permanent implants.
Surgical removal of a discrete mass.

Dilation of the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle of the heart by inflating a balloon.
Dilation of the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle of the heart by use of a surgeon's finger or rigid instrument.
Surgery performed for the purpose of reducing regurgitation of the mitral valve.
Surgery performed with the purpose of replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, dysfunctional, etc. mitral valve with bioprosthetic, homograft or autograft valve.
Surgical removal of one or both breasts, including the areola, nipple, and the majority of the axillary lymph nodes, but sparing the pectoralis major muscle.

A dermatologic procedure used to treat certain forms of skin cancer in which tissue is removed and immediately tested via frozen section; tissue continues to be removed until clear margins are achieved.

CDISC Synonym(s): Magnetic Resonance Imaging; MRIs; sMRI; Structural MRI
CDISC Definition: Imaging that uses radiofrequency waves and a strong magnetic field rather than x-rays to provide amazingly clear and detailed pictures of internal organs and tissues. The technique is valuable for the diagnosis of many pathologic conditions, including cancer, heart and vascular disease, stroke, and joint and musculoskeletal disorders.

CDISC Synonym(s): Gated Heart Pool Scan; Radionuclide Ventriculogram Scan; Radionuclide Ventriculography; RNV Scan
CDISC Definition: A multi-gated acquisition (MUGA) scan and a form of radionuclide imaging that provides a comprehensive look at blood flow and the function of the lower chambers of the heart ventricles.
An operative procedure that does not involve the heart or the blood vessels.
A type of mechanical ventilation procedure that uses a non-invasive means, such as a face mask or nasal mask, to deliver oxygenated air into the lungs.
A procedure involving an electronic device that delivers electrical stimulation to the heart to treat bradycardia.
Placement of a stent within the pancreas.
Surgical removal of the head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine (duodenum), the gallbladder and the bile duct. (Mayo Clinic)

A biospecimen collection and staining procedure in which secretions and superficial cells of the cervix are collected and stained with the Papanicolaou stain followed by microscopic examination to identify the presence of abnormal cells.
Surgical removal of part of the pancreas.

A percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the placement of an angioplasty guide wire, balloon, or other device (e.g. stent, atherectomy, brachytherapy, or thrombectomy catheter) into a native coronary artery or coronary artery bypass graft for the purpose of mechanical coronary revascularization. Examples of things not considered to be PCI procedures include intravascular ultrasound, measurements of coronary flow reserve, or measurements of fractional flow reserve.
Invasive procedure through a puncture in the skin, performed for the purpose of reducing regurgitation of the mitral valve.

A minimally invasive procedure in which a catheter is inserted into the femoral artery or vein in order to temporarily connect a mechanical circulatory support device that is worn outside the body to the circulatory system.
Removal or resection of the pericardium.
A procedure in which an opening is made in the pericardium.
The aspiration of excess fluid between the pericardium and the heart.
A therapeutic procedure that involves the transplantation of stem cells harvested from the circulating blood of a patient or donor.

A peripheral vascular intervention is a catheter-based or open surgical procedure designed to improve arterial or venous blood flow or otherwise modify or revise vascular conduits. In general, the intention to perform percutaneous vascular intervention is denoted by the insertion of a guide wire into an artery or vein. For the sake of simplicity, this definition applies to the extracranial carotid artery and other non-cardiac arteries and veins, while it excludes the lymphatics and intracranial vessels.
The collection of blood from a vein, most commonly via needle venipuncture.
Use of light and photosensitizing agents to treat cancer and other conditions.
The process by which an image is acquired by recording light emissions.
The treatment of a disorder by exposure to light, including ultraviolet and infrared radiation. (Bartleby.com)
A systemic evaluation of the body and its functions using visual inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation.
The surgical removal of all or part of the pleura. (NCI)
A therapeutic surgical procedure in which the pleural space is surgically eliminated by the adherence of the visceral and parietal pleurae. (NCI)
Surgical removal of a polypoid lesion from the mucosal surface.
Any type of non-invasive mechanical ventilation procedure that uses positive airway pressure to support spontaneous breathing activity.
Surgery performed with the purpose of replacing a degenerated, calcified, malformed, dysfunctional, etc. pulmonary valve with bioprosthetic, homograft or autograft valve.
Dilation of the valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery of the heart by inflating a balloon.
A procedure to block the lacrimal puncta and prevent tear drainage, either manually or with a device.

Surgical removal of one or both breasts, including the areola, nipple, axillary lymph nodes, and pectoral muscles.
Use of targeted or whole body radiation to treat a disease.
Surgical removal of a structure or organ, which was not completely removed in an earlier attempt.
Surgical restoration of form and/or function of a body part.
Any of the procedures used to supplement or substitute for the blood-filtering function of the kidneys.
Surgical removal of the right portion of the colon.
A procedure involving the implantation of a mechanical pump which receives blood from the right ventricle and delivers it to the pulmonary artery.

An imaging technique that uses a small dose of a radioactive chemical (isotope) called a tracer that can detect sites of cancer growth, trauma, infection or degenerative disorders. (NCI)
Surgical removal of a segment of an organ or partial resection of a gland.
Surgical removal and examination of the lymph node which is first in receiving the lymphatic drainage of a specified anatomic location.

Surgical removal of thin slices of tissue from a structure or organ, done with a razor blade or scalpel.
Surgical removal of the sigmoid colon.
A dual-modality imaging technique that merges data from single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and computed tomography (CT) to provide structural and functional information.
NCI Preferred Term: Single Photon Tomography and Computed Tomography Scan

CDISC Definition: The creation of an artificially induced skin blister by the application of mechanical pressure to an area of skin, causing in vivo separation of the epidermis and dermis.

The removal of excess fluid via needle puncture from the thoracic cavity.

Creation of a surgical opening into the trachea.
Use of a thin tube to deliver an artificial valve apparatus between the left ventricle of the heart and the aorta.

A non-invasive cardiac ultrasound performed by placing the transducer on the chest.

A therapeutic procedure that involves the transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells collected from the umbilical cord or placenta.

A special-purpose domain that contains comments that may be collected alongside other data.

An events domain that contains information encompassing and representing data related to subject disposition.

A study reference dataset that provides a consistent identifier (STOCONID) for the representation of a set of environmental conditions under which a test article is stored, and contains a list of those conditions.

The physical state or quality of a biological specimen.
A specimen that has undergone agglutination, a process by which particles collect to form a cohesive mass or cluster.
A specimen that has undergone autolysis, or self-digestion by the specimen's own digestive enzymes. (NCI)
A specimen that has undergone calcification. (NCI)
A specimen that has been cauterized.
A specimen that has become coagulated. (NCI)
A specimen that has undergone concentration to increase the content of a targeted entity.
The presence of any substance or organism that makes a preparation impure. (NCI)
A specimen that has been reduced in strength or concentration by the addition of diluent.
A specimen that has become desiccated or dehydrated.
A specimen that has been preserved in a fixative solution.
A specimen that is analyzed in the state that it was collected.
A specimen that has been subjected to and immobilized by severe cold. (NCI)
A specimen that has a gelatinous consistency. (NCI)
A specimen that has undergone the destruction of red blood cells followed by the release of the hemoglobin. (NCI)
A specimen that exhibits a yellowish pigmentation due to jaundice. (NCI)
A specimen that has become or appears milky.
A specimen that consists of or contains excessive amounts of fat and fatty substances. (NCI)
A specimen that has not undergone the destruction of red blood cells followed by the release of the hemoglobin.
A specimen that has been fixed and preserved in paraffin.
A specimen that has undergone precipitation, a process by which solids are settled out of a solution.
A specimen that has been kept or preserved at a low temperature in a refrigerator. (NCI)

CDISC Synonym(s): Specimen at Ambient Temperature; Specimen at Room Temperature
CDISC Definition: A specimen that has been subjected to and adjusted to the average ambient temperature of a room, usually considered to be around 20 degrees C (68 degrees F). (NCI)
A specimen that has a regular, firm consistency and retains a definite size and shape.
A specimen that has changed from a frozen to a liquid or semi-liquid state.

CDISC Synonym(s): Specimen with Atypical Color; Specimen with Unexpected Color
CDISC Definition: A specimen that has an unanticipated color.
A specimen that has an unanticipated odor.
The name and description of a biological specimen.
The fluid that is abnormally collected in localized areas of damaged tissue within the body, usually composed of living and dead white blood cells, bacteria, and dead tissue.
Connective tissue consisting primarily of adipocytes (fat cells) and supporting structural matrix.
The gas from the alveoli of the lungs.
The fluid within the amniotic cavity which surrounds and protects the developing embryo. (NCI)
The watery fluid which is present in the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye. (NCI)

Oxygenated blood which is transported with nutrients to body tissues through the arterial system. The exception is blood within the pulmonary artery which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. (NCI)
Blood present in the umbilical arteries at the time of delivery.
A plasma sample that is prepared from arterial blood.
Capillary blood collected from a puncture site that has been warmed or treated with creams containing a hyperemic or vasodilatory agent to increase arterial blood flow.
Fatty tissue which is deposited in the inner lining of the arterial wall. (NCI)
A type of tear produced continually to keep the cornea moist; contains salts, water, and mucus.
Fluid composed of waste products, bile acids, salts, cholesterol, and electrolytes. It is produced by the liver and may be stored in the gallbladder (if present).

A liquid tissue with the primary function of transporting oxygen and carbon dioxide. It supplies the tissues with nutrients, removes waste products, and contains various components of the immune system defending the body against infection.
Any cell with a single nucleus found in the bone marrow, for example lymphocytes, monocytes, mesenchymal stem cells and hematopoietic progenitor cells.
The tissue occupying the spaces of some bones. It consists of blood vessel sinuses and a network of hematopoietic cells.
The solid, spongey portion of bone marrow, consisting of blood vessel sinuses, hematopoietic cells, and trabecular bone.
The liquid portion of bone marrow, consisting of small tissue fragments, hematopoietic cells, and peripheral blood.
Calcified connective tissue that forms the skeletal components of the body. (NCI)
A liquid produced by the mammary gland.
The middle fraction of an anticoagulated blood specimen following separation by centrifugation. It contains most of the white blood cells and platelets.
A concretion of material in the body, usually composed of mineral salts. Representative examples include gallbladder stones, kidney stones, and salivary gland stones.
A mixture of arterial blood, venous blood and interstitial fluid, which is found in the capillaries.
A plasma sample that is prepared from capillary blood.
The striated muscle tissue of the heart enveloped by the epicardium and the endocardium. (NCI)
A cell sample that has been compacted by centrifugation.
The fluid that is contained within the brain ventricles, the subarachnoid space and the central canal of the spinal cord. (NCI)
A wax secreted by glands in the ear canal.
The watery fluid secreted from the glands and associated structures of the cervicovaginal region.
A metastatic cancer cell found in the peripheral blood. (NCI)
A thick, protein-rich substance secreted by the breasts during the second half of pregnancy and for a few days after birth before the breast milk comes in.
Blood present in the umbilical vessels at the time of delivery.
The fluid (acellular) portion of the circulating blood with retained clotting components from the cord blood of a newborn baby.
The clear portion of the blood that remains after the removal of the blood cells and the clotting proteins from the cord blood of a newborn baby.

The cells and connective tissue from the inner layer of the two main layers of the skin. The dermis has connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, hair follicles, and other structures. It is made up of a thin upper layer called the papillary dermis, and a thick lower layer called the reticular dermis.
The fluid which runs through a dialysis machine and captures, for discard or analysis, the excess water and waste from the blood stream through diffusion and ultrafiltration. (NCI)
The dialysis fluid which is collected from the peritoneal space and captures, for discard or analysis, the excess water and waste from the blood stream through diffusion and ultrafiltration. (NCI)
Normal or abnormal secretions expelled from a body location.

Endogenously generated droplets present in exhaled air, containing water and non-volatile material, which originate from the surfactant and respiratory tract lining fluid from the most distal airways.
Partially digested gastric contents that are returned to the mouth or beyond via the vomit reflex present in some species.
A type of tear produced in response to negative or positive emotions; contains higher amounts of proteins and stress-related hormones in comparison to other tear types.
A specimen that consists of the cells and connective tissue of the endometrium.

CDISC Synonym(s): Endotracheal Aspirate Fluid; ETA Fluid; Tracheal Aspirate; Tracheal Aspirate Fluid
CDISC Definition: The fluid collected from the lumen of the trachea.

The cells and connective tissue from the epithelial portion of the skin (cutis). It consists of the following layers: stratum corneum (horny layer), stratum granulosum (granular layer), stratum spinosum (prickle cell layer), and stratum basale (basal cell layer).
Any of the cells of the epithelium, which covers the body and lines its cavities and glands.
Cell specialized for oxygen transport, having a high concentration of hemoglobin in the cytoplasm and little else; biconcave, anucleate discs, 7nm diameter in mammals.
Expired air that has been condensed.
The air that moves out of the chest during expiration. It contains a higher percentage of carbon dioxide and a lower percentage of oxygen compared to the inhaled air. (NCI)
Accumulation of extravasated fluid containing inflammatory cells and fibrin. Necrotic debris and/or other cellular and extracellular components may also be present.
A connective tissue cell that secretes collagen, a component of the extracellular matrix.
Liquid substances produced by the body.
The contents of the stomach that may include undigested food mixed with juices secreted by the gastric mucosal glands. (NCI)
The fluid produced by the stomach glands, composed of gastric acids and enzymes. (NCI)
A type of leukocyte containing a nucleus and cytoplasmic granules. Granulocytes are subdivided according to the staining properties of their granules into eosinophils, basophils, and neutrophils.

A tube-like invagination of the epidermis from which the hair shaft develops and into which the sebaceous glands open; the follicle is lined by a cellular inner and outer root sheath of epidermal origin and is invested with a fibrous sheath derived from the dermis. (NCI)
The filamentous outgrowth of the epidermis. (NCI)
The liquid, solid or semi-solid lying below a liquid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a plasma sample. (NCI)
The liquid, solid or semi-solid lying below a liquid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a pleural fluid sample. (NCI)
The liquid, solid or semi-solid lying below a liquid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a serum sample. (NCI)
The extracellular fluid component found in the spaces between tissues. This excludes plasma and transcellular fluid.
A specific individual microbe and its genetically identical progeny separated on a single occasion from a sample taken from a host or culture system.
The keratin-producing cell of the epidermis that forms in the deep basal layer of the stratified epithelium.
Fluid introduced and collected from a body cavity or location by lavage or wash procedure.
Blood cells that are devoid of hemoglobin, capable of amoeboid motion and phagocytosis, and act as the principal components of the immune system.
Vaginal discharge occurring during the post-partum period. It consists of a mixture of blood, mucus, and placental remnants. (NCI)

Pulmonary surfactant lines the lung epithelium and lowers surface tension to prevent collapse at end-expiration. Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant results in respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in premature infants. Lung surfactant is synthesized in alveolar type II cells, stored in lamellar bodies and secreted via exocytosis. (NCI)
Tissue composed of specialized cells that are organized as a definite organ, situated along the course of lymphatic vessels, and consisting of an outer cortical and an inner medullary part.

A clear, transparent, sometimes faintly yellow and slightly opalescent fluid that is collected from the tissues throughout the body, flows in the lymphatic vessels (through the lymph nodes), and is eventually added to the venous blood circulation. Lymph consists of a clear liquid portion, varying numbers of white blood cells (chiefly lymphocytes), and a few red blood cells. (NCI)

White blood cells formed in the body's lymphoid tissue. The nucleus is round or ovoid with coarse, irregularly clumped chromatin while the cytoplasm is typically pale blue with azurophilic (if any) granules.
The cellular debris and fluid produced by lysis of cells.
The newborn's first intestinal discharge. It is a dark-green, thick substance composed of mucus, intestinal secretions, hair, and intestinal mucosa cells. (NCI)
The discharged blood from the uterus during the reproductive years. The discharge occurs approximately once a month. (NCI)
The de-oxygenated blood flowing into the right side of the heart, composed of a mixture of venous blood from the entirety of the systemic circulation.

A large, phagocytic mononuclear leukocyte produced in the vertebrate bone marrow and released into the blood; containing a large, oval or somewhat indented nucleus surrounded by voluminous cytoplasm and numerous organelles.
The thick fluid secreted by the mucus glands in the aerodigestive tract and the vagina. (NCI)
Tissue responsible for body and internal organ movement. Muscle tissue is composed of specialized contractile cells.
The cutaneous plate on the dorsal surface of the distal end of a finger or toe. (NCI)

Cells resembling large granular lymphocytes that do not express markers of either T or B cell lineage. These cells express Fc receptors for IgG and can kill target cells using antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. They can also use perforin to kill cells in the absence of antibody, and may occur without previous sensitization.
The fluid within the pericardial cavity.
A peripheral blood cell with a single nucleus, for example lymphocytes and monocytes.
An immature (progenitor) cell circulating in the peripheral blood. It has the capacity for replication and differentiation to mature blood cells.
The fluid within the peritoneal cavity.
The liquid secreted by the sweat glands. (NCI)
The fluid that is produced from the movement of whole blood across a semipermeable membrane in response to a pressure gradient, removing blood cells and large proteins.
The fluid (acellular) portion of the circulating blood with retained clotting components.
A plasma sample that is prepared from whole blood, which has undergone a number of centrifugation steps to decrease the amount of platelets. (NCI)
A plasma sample that is prepared from whole blood, which has undergone a number of centrifugation steps to concentrate the amount of platelets. (NCI)
An irregular, disc-shaped structure in the blood that assists in blood clotting. Platelets are not blood cells, they are fragments of large bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes. (NCI)
The fluid within the pleural cavity.
The serous membrane that lines the wall of the thoracic cavity and the surface of the lungs.
A slightly alkaline, white fluid secreted from the prostate and is a constituent of semen.
A yellowish substance produced during bacterial inflammation. It contains necrotic cells and cells fighting the infection. (NCI)
A type of tear produced in response to irritation from foreign particles, vapors, bright lights, or peppery substances; contains higher amounts of antibodies in comparison to other tear types.
Immature erythrocytes that have just undergone extrusion of their cell nucleus. They still contain some organelles that gradually decrease in number as the cells mature.
A clear liquid secreted by the salivary glands.
A thick, oily substance produced by the sebaceous glands located in the dermis. (NCI)
The fluid containing the spermatozoa, secreted by the testes and accessory reproductive glands of the male.
Part of the ejaculated fluid. It contains secretions from the seminal vesicles, Cowper gland, and prostate gland.
A specimen type consisting of serum or plasma or blood.
The non-cellular portion of the circulating blood, with or without the clotting proteins present.
The clear portion of the blood that remains after the removal of the blood cells and the clotting proteins. (NCI)
Voluntary, striated muscle tissue predominantly associated with the skeleton.
Tissue composed of three layers, epidermis, dermis and subcutis which protect underlying muscles and organs.
A white secretion of the sebaceous glands of the foreskin. (NCI)
Primarily involuntary, non-striated muscle tissue of the internal organs and blood vessels.
Refers to muscle, fat, fibrous tissue, blood vessels, organ parenchyma, or other supporting tissue of the body.
The male reproductive cell that is formed in the testicle. A sperm consists of a head, a body, and a tail that provides propulsion.
Material containing mucus, cellular debris, microorganisms and sometimes blood or pus. It is ejected through the mouth from the lungs, bronchi, and trachea. (NCI)
The material discharged from the bowel during defecation. It consists of undigested food, intestinal mucus, epithelial cells, and bacteria. (NCI)

Striated muscles are appendicular and axial muscles typically connected at either or both ends to the bony skeleton of the body. Striated muscle fibers contain a highly organized, contractile cytoskeletal apparatus with a striated microscopic appearance; muscle contraction is typically under voluntary control. (NCI)
The liquid lying above a liquid, solid or semi-solid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a cerebrospinal fluid sample. (NCI)
The liquid lying above a liquid, solid or semi-solid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a lavage fluid sample.
The liquid lying above a liquid, solid or semi-solid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a peritoneal fluid sample. (NCI)
The liquid lying above a liquid, solid or semi-solid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a plasma sample. (NCI)
The liquid lying above a liquid, solid or semi-solid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a pleural fluid sample. (NCI)
The liquid lying above a liquid, solid or semi-solid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a serum or plasma sample. (NCI)
The liquid lying above a liquid, solid or semi-solid residue, which is separated by crystallization, precipitation or centrifugation of a serum sample. (NCI)
A heterogeneous and variable aggregate of body fluids, tissues, cells, microorganisms, and other materials that are collected from a swab biospecimen collection procedure.
The fluid within a joint capsule.
The fluid secreted by the lacrimal apparatus.
An anatomical structure consisting of similarly specialized cells and intercellular matrix, aggregated according to genetically determined spatial relationships, performing a specific function. (NCI)
The fluid that passes through the wall of the veins and capillaries to the surrounding tissues because of increased intravascular pressure. It has low protein content. (NCI)
A tumor sample, or entire tumor that is removed for examination.
Material separated from urine.
The fluid produced by the kidneys.

Deoxygenated blood containing urea and other waste products which is transported through the venous system to the heart and lungs. The exception is blood within the pulmonary vein which is oxygenated and travels from the lungs to the left atrium of the heart. (NCI)
Blood present in the umbilical vein at the time of delivery.
A plasma sample that is prepared from venous blood.
The clear colorless transparent jelly that fills the posterior chamber of the eyeball. (NCI)

The nerve tissue forming the bulk of the deep parts of the brain and the superficial parts of the spinal cord. It is composed of nerve cell processes, i.e. extensions (axons), which connect various gray matter areas of the brain to each other and carry nerve impulses to and from the nerve cell bodies within the central nervous system (neurons). (NCI)
A terminology codelist relevant to the nature of the investigation for which study information is being collected.

Studies that provide a means for obtaining an experimental drug or device for patients who are not adequately treated by existing therapy, who do not meet the eligibility criteria for enrollment, or who are otherwise unable to participate in another clinical study.

Studies in which individuals are assigned by an investigator based on a protocol to receive specific interventions. Subjects may receive diagnostic, therapeutic or other types of interventions. The assignment of the intervention may or may not be random. The individuals are then followed and biomedical and/or health outcomes are assessed.

Study in which the researchers observe the effect of a risk factor (e.g., exposure), diagnostic test, treatment or other covariate within a study population, and where the investigator does not assign specific interventions. (CDISC Glossary)

Observational studies which include an organized system that uses observational methods to collect uniform data (clinical and other) prospectively for a population defined by a particular disorder/disease, condition (including susceptibility to a disorder), or exposure (including products, health care services, and/or procedures) and that serves a predetermined scientific, clinical, or policy purpose. Patient registries may be single purpose or on-going data collection programs that address one or more questions. (AHRQ)
Terminology relevant to the subcategory for disposition events.
NCI Preferred Term: CDISC SDTM Subcategory for Disposition Event Terminology

CDISC Definition: The act of taking part in a study.
The act of taking part in the treatment phase of a study.
The test code representing each subject characteristic.
NCI Preferred Term: CDISC SDTM Subject Characteristic Test Code Terminology

NCI Preferred Term: Number of First Degree Biological Relatives

CDISC Definition: The number of brothers that are biologically related to the subject. (NCI)
The number of sisters that are biologically related to the subject. (NCI)
The name of the country in which the subject was born.

CDISC Synonym(s): Birth Country Code; Country of Birth Code
CDISC Definition: A coded value specifying the name of the country in which the subject was born.
An indication as to whether the subject was breast fed (received mother's milk) as an infant.
The number of fetuses delivered live or dead at any time in the pregnancy, regardless of gestational age or if the fetuses were delivered at different dates in the pregnancy. (CDC)
The number of children (including neonates) residing in the household.

An indication as to whether a contact investigation (a public health activity whereby individuals who have been exposed to a person with a suspected or confirmed contagious illness are identified for contact tracing) has been carried out for the subject.
The county identified as the individual's permanent residence.
The appearance of objects (or light sources) described in terms of a person's perception of their hue and lightness (or brightness) and saturation. (NCI)

CDISC Synonym(s): Entry Date from Ptntl Cntry Disease Exp
CDISC Definition: The date on which the subject arrived in the reporting country from the country of potential disease exposure.
NCI Preferred Term: Entry Date from Country of Potential Disease Exposure

CDISC Definition: System of classification based on the nation in which an individual was exposed to a disease, regardless of the nation in which he/she currently resides.
The country identified as the individual's permanent residence.
An indication as to whether the individual is enrolled at a daycare facility.
The conditions under which an organ is harvested from a dead donor, including the condition of the donor and the environment.
The district in which the individual was potentially exposed to a disease.
The district identified as the individual's permanent residence.

CDISC Synonym(s): Donor Status at Time of Organ Donation
CDISC Definition: The donor's state or condition of being either living or brain dead at the time of organ harvesting.
NCI Preferred Term: Donor Status at Time of Organ Donation

CDISC Definition: A characterization or classification of the physical location where the individual resides.
An approximate calculation of the delivery date.
Highest level of education that a person has attained.
The number of years of education that a person has completed.
An approximate calculation of the gestational age of the fetus, neonate, or infant.

CDISC Synonym(s): Employee Job; Occupation; Type of Work
CDISC Definition: A code specifying the job performed by the employee for the employer. For example, accountant, programmer analyst, patient care associate, staff nurse, etc.
The state or condition of an individual's employment.
The status of an individual with respect to their ability to produce offspring.
An indication as to whether the subject is a full-time student.

A person's internally held sense of their gender, which may or may not correspond to the individual's genotypic or phenotypic sex. CDISC Definition: The gestational age of the subject at birth.
The preferred hand of use for controlled and efficient performance of motor tasks.
An indication as to whether the subject is covered by their own or a family member's employer-based health insurance.
An indication as to whether the subject is covered by their own or a family member's U.S. Indian Health Service insurance.
An indication as to whether the subject is covered by health insurance.
An indication as to whether the subject is covered by their own or a family member's military-based health insurance.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. MMWR Recomm Rep 1994; 43: 1-17).

CDISC Definition: An indication of the position on a scale measuring revenue or monetary support.

CDISC Definition: An indication as to whether the subject is less than one year of age.

CDISC Definition: An indication as to whether the participant or subject has been diagnosed as intersex.
The longest amount of time during which the individual abstained from an activity.
The main language that is spoken by the subject most frequently or dominantly.
Additional language(s) that is spoken by the subject but not considered the primary language.
An indication as to whether the associated person is living with the subject. (NCI)
The state or condition of a person's matrimonial status.
An indication as to whether the subject is covered by Medicaid.
An indication as to whether the subject is covered by Medicare.
The status of an individual with regard to military service.
System of classification based on nation from which a person originates, regardless of the nation in which he/she currently resides.

CDISC Synonym(s): Business Type; Occupation Type; Occupational Industry; Work Industry
CDISC Definition: Type of business that compensates for work or assigns work to an unpaid worker or volunteer. (USCDI)
A description of the subject's lifestyle with respect to physical activity.
The total number of people residing in the household.
An indication as to whether the subject was born prior to 37 weeks and 0 days gestation.
The categorization of individuals with or without the potential for having a particular disease.
An indication that a subject is part of a population group that has a greater chance of contracting a disease or disorder.
Social factors such as personal behavior, lifestyle, or environment belonging to the subject which are known to increase the likelihood of infection and disease.
A code specifying the method used by the employer to compute the employee's salary or wages. For example, hourly, annual, or commission.
The environment within which the person may have come into contact with a disease carrier, or played the role of a disease carrier.

The sex assigned to an infant, most often based on the infant's anatomical and other biological characteristics. Sometimes referred to as birth sex, natal sex, biological sex, or sex; however, sex assigned at birth is the recommended term. (Fenway Health)
The pattern of a person's emotional, romantic, and/or sexual attractions.
The status of an individual with regard to secondhand smoke exposure.
Test to categorize the sensitivity of a subject's skin to sunlight. (Fitzpatrick TB. The validity and practicality of sun-reactive skin types I through VI. Arch. Dermatol. 1998 124: 869-871.)
An indication as to whether the fetus or infant is small for the gestational age.
A characterization or classification of an individual that takes into account economics, demographics, and social interactions, used to stratify individual behaviors within a society or culture.

CDISC Synonym(s): State-Specific Health Ins Program Name; State-Specific Health Insurance Program Name
CDISC Definition: The name of the U.S. state-specific health insurance program.
The name of the U.S. state-specific Medicaid program.
The name of the U.S. state-specific Medicare program.
An indication as to whether the subject or associated person is enrolled in school.

An arbitrary categorization of individuals based on the assemblage of physical properties related to reproduction, and commonly associated with the designation of such categories as female and male. This designation is based on some combination of observable information from organ inventories, morphological assessment, hormone assessments, genetic testing, observed primary and secondary sex characteristics, menstrual status, and/or obstetric history. Current sex designation may or may not be the same as an individual's sex assigned or reported at birth. (NCI)
A physical or mental experience or observation reported by a patient that may indicate a disease.
An indication as to whether the individual has received tobacco cessation counseling.
A tribe or band with which a person associates. (USCDI)
The classification of the two offspring born from the same pregnancy.
Identification and clinical investigation of disease contacts.
An indication as to whether the subject is unhoused.
The village identified as the individual's permanent residence.

The initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans. Phase 1 studies are typically closely monitored and may be conducted in patients or normal volunteer subjects. NOTE: These studies are designed to determine the metabolism and pharmacologic actions of the drug in humans, the side effects associated with increasing doses, and, if possible, to gain early evidence on effectiveness. During Phase 1, sufficient information about the drug's pharmacokinetics and pharmacological effects should be obtained to permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies. The total number of subjects and patients included in Phase I studies varies with the drug, but is generally in the range of 20 to 80. Phase 1 studies also include studies of drug metabolism, structure-activity relationships, and mechanism of action in humans, as well as studies in which investigational drugs are used as research tools to explore biological phenomena or disease processes.
